hard_items.why: A ('I want someone to want me') sounds romantic, which is odd for a 67-year-old widow. What she really wants is to be needed, and A only half says that. B ('everything feels heavy') is not how she sees herself either.
Both sides are faults she does not see in herself: replaying arguments (she thinks she never keeps score) and finding correction hard (her bossiness about rice). As herself she would say neither.

B (liking people to know what she has done) is exactly what her friend sees, but she would never admit it. A (putting off what matters) fits the nephew loan only in part. She leans A because B is a side she would not own.

She would deny both wanting her good work noticed and thinking she'd do things better, though both are true of her. Picking either one feels like confessing something she does not believe about herself.
Easy to answer as her, but her answer is wrong. She honestly believes her anger is gone in minutes, yet she keeps a list of slights for years. Self-report will score her the wrong way here.
'Money' really is what nephews come to her for. She would feel it was ungracious to say so, so a real Lola might skip it and pick prayer instead.

He works nights. At three in the morning he is on shift, not lying awake, so the question does not fit his life. What actually keeps him up after shifts is Ellie's question. 'Something someone said or did to you' makes it sound like a grievance, which it is not.
He lives alone and has Ellie every other weekend. 'The people I live with' has no clear answer for him. He means Ellie, but she is exactly the person who walks on eggshells around him.

Neither side fits. He does not stop (the shouting keeps happening), and he does not say sorry properly either: he says 'no hard feelings, yeah?' and buys a can. He leans A only because he knows he is 'not one for saying sorry'.
A puts drink in with food ('something to eat or drink'). So his four or five cans after a shift score the same as a sandwich, and the drinking this quiz ought to catch gets lost.
What he really does is shrug off one person's opinion (Dean on his drinking). He would never admit that, so he answers A, the 'fair enough, pull me aside' answer, and self-report hides the truth.
He is on time and keeps his word, but he blows up over small things like a failing scanner. 'Careful about small things' and 'let small things slide' both half fit, in different senses.
He does neither. He leaves the room. He does not say where he stands and he does not try to calm anyone down. He leans B only because it is the less wrong of the two.
He does not put music on when he is alone. He walks or reads military history. 'Slow and a little sad' vs 'upbeat' has no answer for him.
Long dull tasks do not bother him (rechecking other people's calculations is his job). He would neither go for a snack nor wish he were elsewhere.
Both are hard for him. He guards his emergency savings, and he never changes his mind. As himself he picks A only because he believes he is 'open to other views'.
Praise does not move him and neither does 'you can do better'. What moves him is being shown the numbers. Neither side fits.
Neither side fits. He does not let things slide (he rechecks everything), and he rarely feels anger at all. 'My anger usually feels justified' is true only in a thin sense.
For him, 'think carefully about how to put it' just means being precise, but it reads like spin. A careful, honest man may avoid B for that reason even though B describes his habit.
She rushes into ventures, but she sees herself as short of time, so she would describe her unfinished projects as things she 'never got round to'. Each side fits a different version of the same fact.
When she is worn out she does one more task or cleans. The flirting side does not fit, so food wins only because it is the lesser of two wrong options.
What keeps her awake at night is her ventures and her to-do list. Neither money nor something someone said covers it.
She would not admit to being 'low'. The flat dread she feels on evenings alone fits 'heavy', but she would hesitate to name it that way.
She would claim that a strong argument wins her over. In fact she resists being pushed by anyone, so her self-view and her behaviour point opposite ways.
Her self-image says 'say it straight, I can take it', but she hates being told what to do. It is an easy item to answer aspirationally.
She is a 74-year-old widow and every day is the same, so 'a weekend with nothing planned' means nothing to her. She always has the hens and the grave to see to.
The flirting side is absurd for a widow in black who is grieving her son. She picks A by elimination, not because food pulls at her.
Same problem as x1: 'attention from someone attractive' is unthinkable for her, so B wins by default.
She does not put music on when she is alone. At most there is chant or silence, so the item barely applies.
She neither snacks nor wishes she were elsewhere during dull work. Long dull tasks are simply her life.
She does say cutting things on the spot, but she would never 'wish she hadn't', because she thinks she is only being honest. The regret half of B is false for her, and A is false too.
What keeps her awake at 3 a.m. is grief for her son. Neither money nor someone's words covers it, though her counting of who missed the memorials pulls her towards B.
She lives alone, so 'the people I live with' does not apply. The nearest stand-in is her daughter-in-law, who gets her worst.
Honestly, people hardly come to her for anything. She sends back eggs and oil unasked, so 'giver' is only the nearest fit.
Both sides are true of her. She is closed like a fist about her grief and her anger at God, yet she is openly cutting to Maria.

He never actually has nothing to do, because games and short videos fill every gap. His 'chill' self-view says his thoughts settle, while the truth, which he avoids, is that they get worse. He answered from the self-view.
His self-view says 'it'll all work out', yet he feels anxious about everything ahead of him. The item makes him choose between the persona and the feeling.
When he is worn out he games or scrolls. Neither food nor flirting is really what pulls at him.
At 3 a.m. he is usually still gaming. The worry underneath is his major and falling behind, which is neither money nor something someone said.
His projects die in the middle, around day nine, not at the first step or the last ten percent. A is only the closer of two poor fits.
Both sides are true of him. Replies like 'haha yeah' come out without thought, but he never voices a real opinion he has not turned over, and usually not even then.
People mostly come to him to hang out and for easy company. None of the seven lines names that, so 'caregiver' is a stretch.
He is equally pleasant with customers, his friends and his family, so this is genuinely neither, and he answered 0.

She knows the patients get her best and the family gets the sergeant, but her self-view says she is fair to everyone and firm at home only because someone has to be. She would hesitate between the honest answer and the answer that fits her picture of herself.

Neither side fits. She does not stop, because the evening scolding happens again the next day, and she does not say sorry either. Side A's 'I stop doing it' is false, and B's 'quick to say sorry' is false too.
She finishes things and starts fast, so neither the last ten percent nor the first step feels hard to her. It had to be 0.
She does not drift during dull work, she just pushes through. Both the snack and the 'anywhere else' feel like someone else's habits.

Both are true. She hides her tiredness from everyone, but she also tells Peter and the junior nurses exactly what she thinks, sometimes at the wrong moment. The item mixes hiding feelings with blurting opinions.
She runs the ward in front of everyone, but most of her care is unseen: covering the juniors, three a.m. hand-holding. 'Useful' could honestly go either way.
He almost never leaves things undone. His problem is never feeling finished and redoing other people's work, so neither 'never got started' nor 'lost steam' describes him.
He believes everything he does is for his family, so he would want to say B. He also half knows he is on his phone and absent at home. Neither side captures 'I work for them but I'm not with them'.
His anger goes cold, not hot, and he comes home drained. 'Angry' and 'low' both miss the cold, tense, distracted state he actually ends up in.
He hardly puts music on at all. His late-night release is variety shows, so the item has nothing to grip.
He does not put off work, and he would not say he wants recognition, even though he fears being passed over. Both sides feel slightly wrong. He would pick B only because A is more clearly false.
He neither apologises readily nor clearly stops. He goes cold and carries on, so A was the nearer of two poor fits.
He copes with a pile-up and even prefers busyness to idleness, but the dread comes before he starts. 'Buried' and 'come alive' both overstate one half.
Both are real. The bank app frightens her, but she avoids thinking about money on purpose, and she stews over rude clients and feeling judged at church. Only 0 felt honest.
Food fits (a diet every Monday), but she also loves quickly and a man from church is messaging her. The flirting side is one she would be embarrassed to admit even when it is partly true.
Both are true. She cries alone on the back step, when everything feels heavy, and she also wants to be wanted and liked. Picking one felt arbitrary.
Her flare is over quickly, but she stews for a day afterwards, mostly out of regret. It is unclear whether that stewing counts as the anger lasting.
She decides fast and feels like a fighter, yet she trusts too fast and gets swayed. Her self-view and her record point different ways.
After a bad day with people she flares up and then gets low, often in the same evening. The item forces one of the two.

As a fighter she would say 'say it straight'. But she is embarrassed to accept even kindly offered budget help and feels judged easily, so her self-image and her real sensitivity pull in opposite directions.

A 78-year-old man married 54 years feels no pull from either one. Attention from someone attractive is unthinkable to him, and praise from someone important is exactly the fuss he avoids, so he can only answer 0.
What keeps him up at 3am is June's decline and the aide decision. Neither money nor something someone said fits. He picked money only because memory care costs are tied to it.
After 42 years at a mill he just keeps going at a dull task. He neither goes for a snack nor wishes he were elsewhere, so the forced lean toward a coffee is weak.

People come to him for a hand: moving a couch, mowing the lawn, fixing something. The list has no practical-help option. He would not say people come to him for care, money, teaching or someone to take charge, so he picked none.
He sees himself as needing neither. Admitting he needs a push (the knee, the aide) is the insight his son has, not him. B wins only because A plainly does not fit.
Both sides feel boastful to a man who wants no fuss. He does quietly think he looks after June better than a stranger would, but he would never call it 'doing most things better than others'.
A week of people and plans would tire him out, and a week with nothing to do would drive him up the wall. The item mixes being worn out with being restless.

Both sides are true of her. She says almost nothing about herself, which is A, and she makes cutting remarks at the wrong moment, which is B. Her self-image as the blunt one pushes B, but the item hides a real split.
Both sides are true again. Her remarks upset people without her noticing, and she is easily hurt. Her self-view as the unsentimental realist fights the B answer she half knows is right.
Her self-view says she doesn't care what people think. The online arguments she replays in bed say otherwise. The honest answer as she sees herself (A) and the truth pull opposite ways.
Neither pulls at her. She would sneer at praise from someone important, and attention from someone attractive is a small, vain pull at most. The lean is weak and close to made up.
Her mood is sardonic: jokes laid over a gloomy outlook. 'Light' and 'serious' split one thing that for her is a single blend.
She laughs everything off out loud and then lies awake with it. The item asks which one, and her self-image and her habits give opposite answers.

A devout Orthodox man who fasts would not admit to 'flirting', though he does think about the kind young woman at church. Food is the side he can admit to, especially on fast days, so he leans A even though B has some truth in it.

He would say 'let me think' and check his spreadsheet. The reason is the $600 his mother and sisters need, not 'I need to know I'll be okay'. His own needs always come last, so A's stated reason is wrong for him.
On fast days, twelve hours at the wheel, a snack isn't allowed, and he is too dutiful to dwell on wishing he were elsewhere. Neither side fits, so the lean is thin.
When he is alone he listens to church songs. They are slow and mournful, but he would not call them 'sad', and they are certainly not upbeat.

He gives to his family all the time, so giving isn't hard. He also doesn't see himself as someone who won't admit another way is better. Other drivers call him stubborn, but he sees that as principle.
Both sides feel proud to him. He does quietly think he drives more honestly than other drivers, but he would hesitate to own 'I'd do most things better than others'.
He never argues out loud. What he replays is irritation he never said, not arguments. And he believes he takes correction well, so both sides are a stretch.
A week of people wears him down, but home means noisy roommates and guilt about being idle. The word 'home' doesn't mean rest for him.
When she is worn out she goes for a run. Neither food nor flirting pulls at her, so she picked A only because B fits her even less.
She holds back out of guilt and having no money. The reason in B, 'don't want to go soft', is a toughness motive she would never say about herself.
Neither is hard for her. She gives things away too easily and admits someone else was right far too quickly, so the item finds nothing to measure.
She does not judge other people's eating, but she also thinks twice about everything. 'Don't think twice about it' in B is exactly what she can't do.
What keeps her awake is something SHE said and whether she offended someone, not something done to her. B is only the closer of two wrong answers.
'Gets the best of you' can also mean 'beats you' ('curiosity got the best of me'). She had to guess which meaning was intended.
A free weekend feels like a gift because she is exhausted, but idle time makes her thoughts worse. The two items pull against each other and she answered them differently.
People come to her to talk, to tell her things they tell no one else. There is no 'someone to listen' line, so caregiver has to stand in for it.
What keeps him awake is his son at the front, and neither side offers that. Money is only the nearer of two wrong answers.
In a dull task he goes out for a cigarette. A snack is the closest option, but that is not what he actually does.
A man like him barely puts music on; he sits in the car in silence. The question assumes a habit he doesn't have.
His self-image is a man who needs nobody to slow him down or push him. Both sides ask him to admit a need he would deny.
Neither moves him: he does the job right whatever anyone says. This was a true 'neither', so he answered 0.
He doesn't look back at regrets, and his real one (the drinking) was neither rushed into nor something he never got round to.
He notices that he is paid less than the Polish men, but that is about unfairness, not about someone doing better than him. And he is not the admiring type either.
His kindness is hands-on and practical, like fixing a car for nothing, and no line offers that. Giver and shepherd are rough stand-ins.
What keeps her awake is her parents' health and her son's reading. Neither side names it, and money only half fits.
She is rarely low. When she is, she gets busy and forgets, and 'I want someone to want me' reads oddly for a settled married mother. Neither side really fits her.
When work piles up she just gets on with it. She neither feels buried nor comes alive, so any lean is weak.
She makes up by morning and takes correction at work without fuss, so neither side is her.
Her pattern is starting well every January and fading around the middle of the year. That is neither 'the last ten percent' nor 'the first step'.
Her friends come to her as the sensible one, for level-headed advice, and no line offers that. Teacher is the nearest stand-in.
Neither attention from someone attractive nor praise from someone important is his pull; his is food and being the big-hearted host, so the pick is nearly arbitrary.
He does not see himself as someone who gets low; when he does he eats or works, and neither option describes that.
What drives him is providing for his family, which is neither fear of letting people down nor a chance to shine; he would hesitate between the two.
Customers and delivery men really get his best while his kids miss him, but his self-view as a good provider makes 'the people I live with' feel like the answer he ought to give.

'Let things slide' could mean his health (true, but he doesn't see it) or other people's faults (not him); the item's meaning is unclear, and his anger is not something he calls justified or unjustified, just how men in his family are.
Both are true of him: he wants his hard work seen and he distrusts his son's ideas, but nothing Luis does is 'quiet', so option B's wording doesn't fit him.
She lives alone with a cat, so 'the people I live with' has no referent; her sister, who gets her worst, doesn't live with her.
She would do neither: she has an opinion but stays silent in groups, so she ends up at 0 by default, not by choice.
Flirting or daydreaming about someone is absurd for her and food isn't really her comfort either; she picks A only because B is impossible.
Long dull tasks don't bother her; she likes order and routine, so neither 'a snack' nor 'wishing I were anywhere else' is her.
She believes she is tolerant yet reports the neighbour's recycling; 'heat rise' is the wrong word for her cold disapproval, and 'give people room' contradicts what she does.
She doesn't gladly do things for people she'd have to be with; her real kindness (soup, feeding a cat, unannounced) doesn't match any line well. Host and caregiver both involve company she avoids.
She denies being low at all; 'I want someone to want me' is the loneliness she won't admit, so she drifts to B by elimination.
She doesn't confront face to face (she goes to the building manager), yet she is sharp and would not simply let it go; the real answer, a cool remark or a later complaint, falls between the options.
When he's worn out his pull is the phone and a bet, which neither food nor flirting captures; he picks food as the less wrong option.
His comfort when low is gambling, not food, and he has no money kept back; neither side is true, and A wins only by elimination.
His 'humble vessel' self-view says fear of letting people down, while the performer who loves the mic would say the chance to shine; he'd be torn and would probably pick the humbler side.
Both fit: he wants his work noticed (performer) and quietly thinks volunteers should do it his way; his humble self-image resists admitting either.
He is plainly most useful on the microphone, but 'just a vessel' pulls him toward saying behind the scenes; the humble self-view makes A feel like boasting.
The pastor in him says let it go; the quick, confident man with an answer for everything would say something; he'd answer by the pastor's ideal, not by what he does.
He hides lows behind extra cheerfulness; privately he feels like a fraud, which is closer to heavy, but wanting to be wanted fits the performer; hard to pick from inside his self-view.
Her answer depends on which group she's in. She is quiet and uses few words in Italian at work, and loud and bossy with the Romanian women at the cafe. 'In a group' does not say which.
Anger flares in her fast (she scrubs the kitchen hard), but she never shows it and answers mildly. The item doesn't say whether it means the feeling or letting it show.
Neither side fits. She is slow to trust men and wants no attention, and there is nobody 'important' whose praise she chases. The answer is forced.

The only person she lives with is her employer, and he gets her patience. The people she loves most (her daughter, her mother) live in another country. So 'the people I live with' doesn't mean what the item intends.
Her gut depends on who is asking. For family she never says no. For a friend she is guarding house money. The item blurs the two.
Almost nothing she is responsible for goes undone. Only her own wishes do, and she wouldn't think of those as 'things that don't get done'.
She is happily married and ordinary. She would say neither attention nor praise pulls at her much. She'd pick one at random.
What really keeps her awake is her mother's heart surgery and her son on his phone. That is neither money nor something said to her. Money (the trailer, the mortgage) comes a distant second.
She truly is both: she clips coupons, then books Cuba on a whim. Neither 'give on impulse' nor 'keep a little back' describes her more than the other.
She doesn't see herself as someone who gets low, only tired and short-tempered. Neither 'want someone to want me' nor 'everything heavy' is how her bad weeks feel.
Neither option is a real struggle for her. The pair tests two unrelated things, so her pick says little.
She gets mad, gets over it, and doesn't replay arguments. Taking correction isn't a big issue for her either. Both sides are weak fits.

She owns the pharmacy, so nobody at work is in charge of her. The one authority she lives under is her father, and she never answers him back. She would tell off an official, though. The item pulls opposite ways.

At 3am she runs disaster scenarios: an explosion, an insulin shortage, her son, Georges in Dubai. That is neither money nor something someone said. She picked money only because the bank collapse is close.
Her lowness comes out as fear, control and rearranging shelves, not as heaviness or wanting to be wanted. Both options miss.
Her self-view says she laughs everything off, and outwardly she does. But she lies awake running scenarios, so things plainly stay with her. Answering from her self-view gives a misleading +2.
She neither treats herself nor holds back on principle. She simply never stops. 'You don't want to go soft' is a motive she doesn't have, and 'treat yourself' isn't really her either.
She snaps at her daughter but swallows her father's criticism for hours. Which side she's on depends on who it is.

Both sides describe him (he wants his giving known, and he thinks he'd run the church and his son's life better). He sees himself as someone who watches his pride, so he can't comfortably pick either.
He is rarely low and sleeps well. Neither 'want someone to want me' nor 'everything feels heavy' fits a contented 71-year-old elder.
Nothing keeps him awake at 3am. Money is not a worry for him, so the answer leans to 'something said' only by default.
He sees himself as disciplined, so neither the snack nor 'wishing I were elsewhere' is something he would own. Both options assume a lapse he wouldn't admit to.
His self-image says 'own it straight away', but he actually deflects with a proverb. Answering honestly from his self-view, without the friend's insight, pulls two ways.
He is personally confident, but he is cautious about new things like the church building and the roof. The item mixes nerve with conservatism.
He doesn't recognise himself as someone things 'go badly' for, so both reactions feel foreign to him.
He would say his anger passes like a good Christian's should, yet the irritation with his son is chronic. It's hard to tell which he would honestly report.
What keeps him up is his father's care, his daughter's exams and his blood pressure. Neither money nor 'something someone said' is it, so 0 is a non-answer rather than a real 'both'.
Both are true of him: he checks the price of cheese, and his doctor wants seven kilos off. The pairing forces a choice between two unrelated habits.
A contented married 50-year-old doesn't feel either pull strongly. The 'attention from someone attractive' side is one few men like him would admit to, which pushes the answer to 'praise' by default.
He is rarely really low. Neither 'want someone to want me' nor 'everything feels heavy' fits an average grumpy-then-cheerful mood.
He isn't much of a praise-seeker or a quiet judge of others. He only leans B because he is stubborn about small things like the dishwasher.
He fixes the same printer every week without fuss. Work piling up neither buries him nor makes him come alive; the extremes don't describe a middle-of-the-road man.
'What you see is what you get' means strangers and family get the same Pieter. Both options assume a split he doesn't have.
He doesn't much replay arguments, and he doesn't mind being disagreed with, yet he is stubborn about small things. Neither side quite fits.
A tired married mother of three feels neither pull. The 'attention from someone attractive' side is one she wouldn't admit to, so 'praise' wins by default.
She is 'blessed, tired, doing fine', not really low. She leans to 'heavy' only because she is tired, not because she is down.
The answer depends on where she is. At work she holds her tongue and complains to Lindiwe later (A); at home she snaps at the children and makes vetkoek (B).
The same split: careful and measured at work, quick to snap at home. One answer can't hold both.
She doesn't feel buried and doesn't 'come alive' either. She just gets on with it, so both options are too dramatic for her.
She quietly judges latecomers but wouldn't call herself better than others. Neither side is how she would put it.
She neither replays arguments nor finds correction hard. She argues with Sipho over money and then laughs, so 0 is a 'neither'.
She doesn't think of herself as having many regrets. Her likely regrets (giving too much money, snapping at the children) are small, not 'rushed into'.
She enjoys both parties and naps. 'Which wears you out faster' mostly measures how tired she is this season, not her temperament.
